name: Heavitree Yew

location.address: St Michael and All Angels churchyard, Church Street, Heavitree, Exeter

official_register.name: Ancient Yew Group database, tree ID 1834

access: Public churchyard, free; the tree stands near the church door.
transport: Heavitree is about 2 km east of Exeter city centre; exact bus stop not verified.

location_site.name: St Michael and All Angels churchyard

how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the yew beside the church door of St Michael and All Angels, one of several yews here. It stands in the churchyard off Church Street, Heavitree.
verify_notes: Girth 307 cm at ground, recorded by Tim Hills 15 May 2004 (AYG ID 1834; coordinate is AYG map pin, grid ref SX93709230, not a tree-level fix). Exeter Trees & Shrubs (local site) calls it the oldest tree in Exeter, 'thought to be over 500 years old'; AYG gives no age. Tree Council named it one of 50 Great British Trees for the 2002 Golden Jubilee (per Wikipedia list and AYG note). Church on the site since at least 1152, church rebuilt in the 19th century; site thought late Saxon; AYG says it will never be known whether this was the head tree (heafod treow) where Saxon kings held court. AYG 2019 report (Heavitree 2019.pdf, text not read) and search snippet: council contractor to remove tarmac on the south footpath and loosen soil over the roots after vehicles drove over the root area. AYG March 2013 post 'Threat to Ancient Heavitree Yew' (content not seen). Alive: lifecheck OLD (2020-04-08, Geograph photo Church Path, Heavitree); AYG 2019 maintenance report implies standing in 2019. Flagged: no photo from the last five years confirmed. Age basis is a local claim, not measured. Writing pass 2026-11-04: lead photo Geograph 7675569 (A J Paxton, 'The Heavitree Yew', taken 2023-09-25) approved; it also shows the tree standing in 2023.
story:
Nobody will ever know whether this is the tree that gave Heavitree its name. The Ancient Yew Group raises the old idea that the suburb was named for a heafod treow, a head tree where Saxon kings held court, and then says plainly that it will never be known whether this yew was it. That is the honest version, and it is a better story than a false certainty.

What is known is enough. Exeter Trees and Shrubs, a local guide, calls it the oldest tree in Exeter, thought to be over 500 years old. That age is their claim, not a measurement, and the trunk is surprisingly slim for it, 307 centimetres at ground level when Tim Hills recorded it in 2004. In 2002 the Tree Council named it one of 50 Great British Trees for the Queen's Golden Jubilee. There has been a church on this site since at least 1152, and the site is thought to be late Saxon, though the present building is 19th century.

The tree has needed help. After vehicles drove over its roots, the council arranged in 2019 for tarmac on the south footpath to be lifted and the soil over the roots loosened. It was photographed standing in 2023.

It stands near the door of St Michael and All Angels, about two kilometres east of the city centre.

name: Kenn Yew

official_register.name: Ancient Yew Group database, tree ID 535

access: Public churchyard, free (AYG: churchyard, public access; owned by the Parochial Church Council).
transport: Kenn is about 9 km south-west of Exeter city centre by road; bus service and walk time not verified, so day-trip fit unconfirmed.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the huge hollow trunk, over ten metres round at the ground, and by the notice board that names it among the oldest in England. It stands in St Andrew's churchyard, Kenn.
verify_notes: Girth 1056 cm at ground, AYG category 'Ancient 7m+', recorded by Tim Hills 7 Feb 1999; Wondermondo also lists 10.06 m at 0.5 m height (2017). AYG cites Swete 1857 journal at 27 ft and a 35 ft measurement; earliest mention Oliver 1840. Age claims differ: church website says the Conservation Foundation certified it over 1000 years old and yew expert Allan Meredith thinks nearer 2000 (church site, not independently dated). AYG: one of few yews with a notice board stating it is among the oldest in England. Church origins 12th century replacing a Saxon building; site may predate Christianity (AYG). Alive: lifecheck RECENT 2025-05-12 (iNaturalist observation 280546975 at the coordinate). Coordinate is the AYG map pin (grid ref SX92198569), not a tree-level fix, but the churchyard is a single glance site. Photo not hunted; AYG photo by Barry Saich 2009 is copyright, not usable. Day-trip distance from Exeter not verified: if transport cannot be stated it still ships as a lone tree page. Writing pass 2026-11-04: lead photo Geograph 1731901 (David Gearing, 'Ancient yew tree in St Andrew, Kenn churchyard', 2008) approved.
story:
The Kenn yew has its own notice board, and the Ancient Yew Group knows of few yews that do. The board calls it among the oldest in England. The tree has the waist to make the case. Tim Hills measured 10.56 metres round at ground level in 1999, and Wondermondo gives 10.06 metres at half a metre up in 2017.

How old that makes it is where the sources part. The church says the Conservation Foundation certified it as over 1,000 years old, and that the yew expert Allen Meredith thinks it nearer 2,000. Neither figure rests on a dating, so we give the range they span and no more. Its paper trail starts in 1840, when Oliver first mentioned it, Swete's journal of 1857 put it at 27 feet, and another record gives 35.

The church of St Andrew dates from the 12th century and replaced a Saxon building, and the Group suggests the site may be older than Christianity here. The yew is huge and hollow, and it has been watched for a long time.

Kenn is a village about 9 kilometres south-west of Exeter city centre by road, not a stroll from town. Check for a bus before you set out, or come by car or bike.
